scenarios.title: Planning Your Study Path
scenarios.situation: You have 3 weeks before your Deep Work interview/exam. You've just opened this bootcamp with 15 domains ahead of you.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective study sequence?
choices: Start Here lessons → core domains in order → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone, doing drills daily
Jump straight to the Mock Assessment to see where you stand
Study only your weakest domain until it's perfect, then move on
Read all lessons first, then do all scenarios, then all labs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The bootcamp is sequenced deliberately: orientation first, then progressive domain mastery with interleaved drills for retention, Systems Anatomy to connect it all, mock under realistic conditions, capstone to prove it. Jumping to the mock wastes its diagnostic value; perfecting one domain starves the others; batching by activity type kills interleaving benefits.
scenarios.hint: What does each phase prepare you for? What happens if you skip the foundation?

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader Trap
scenarios.situation: A learner has 'completed' 40 lessons but fails every scenario. They read each lesson carefully and passed all knowledge checks on the first try.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?
choices: They consumed passively without application — the fix is interleaving scenarios immediately after lessons and doing teach-backs aloud
The lessons are too easy — skip to harder material
They need to re-read the lessons more carefully
Knowledge checks are broken — report a bug
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Passing knowledge checks proves recognition, not application. Scenarios demand transfer — using knowledge in novel situations. The fix is structural: never finish a lesson without immediately attempting its scenarios, and explain each concept aloud (teach-back) to expose shallow understanding.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between recognizing an answer and producing one under pressure?

domains.name: Deep Work: Attention as a Technical Skill
domains.summary: Cal Newport's attention philosophy for technical mastery: the deep work thesis, the rules for focused work, attention training, and building your own study operating system. Original exposition; no book text reproduced.

scenarios.title: Six Interruptions
scenarios.situation: Maya studies distributed systems for three hours. In that time she checks her phone eleven times and answers four messages. She logs the evening as 'three hours of study.'
scenarios.prompt: How should she honestly score that session?
choices: Not three hours of study: every switch leaves attention residue — part of her attention stays on the previous task — so the session was six-plus fragments, each performed with a fraction of her mind. Honest accounting would call it mostly lost.
Three hours. Time at the desk is time studying.
Three hours, because the interruptions were short.
Zero hours — any interruption voids a session entirely.
scenarios.why: Attention residue is the research finding that breaks multitasking: when you switch tasks, leftover attention degrades the new task, and it accumulates with every switch. A session interrupted six times is not six short sessions stitched together; it is six sessions each performed with a fraction of your mind. Protecting the start of a session matters as much as protecting its middle.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of her mind was on Raft consensus during the eleventh phone check?

scenarios.title: Sorting the Work
scenarios.situation: A bootcamp student lists today's tasks: re-derive the proof of a consensus safety property by hand; reorganize study notes into prettier folders; answer forum questions; write a fuzzer and run it until it finds a real crash; reply to group-chat messages.
scenarios.prompt: Which sorting is correct under the deep/shallow distinction?
choices: Deep: re-deriving the proof by hand, writing the fuzzer that finds a real crash. Shallow: reorganizing notes, forum replies, group chat — logistical, interruptible, easy to replicate, and drifting toward the kind of work automation is already eating.
Deep: reorganizing notes and forum replies, because they help others. Shallow: the proof and the fuzzer, because they can wait.
All of it is deep if done with effort.
All of it is shallow unless graded.
scenarios.why: Deep work is professional activity performed in distraction-free concentration that pushes your cognitive capabilities to their limit — it creates new value and is hard to replicate. Shallow work is non-cognitively-demanding, logistical-style work, often performed while distracted, that creates little new value and is easy to replicate. The distinction is economic, not moral: a study life built mostly of shallow work is one automation is already eating.
scenarios.hint: Which tasks would a script do as well as you?

scenarios.title: The Stretchable Day
scenarios.situation: Dev studies 'whenever,' often until 1 a.m., chasing an ever-growing task list. He feels busy but his deep hours are near zero; the day stretches to absorb everything, so nothing is prioritized.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Fixed-schedule productivity: fix the end of the workday, then work backward fitting everything into the hours available. The hard shutdown forces prioritization, saying no, and protecting deep blocks — the opposite of the all-night study session.
Study longer hours to cover the list.
Wake up earlier to add more hours at the front.
Multitask the shallow items into the deep blocks to save time.
scenarios.why: Fixed-schedule productivity is the system Newport actually practices: the constraint forces the discipline. When the day cannot stretch, you must decide what matters. For a learner, the fixed shutdown makes study hours honest — you cannot fake prioritization when 10 p.m. is a wall.
scenarios.hint: What would Dev drop if the day ended at 8 p.m. no matter what?

scenarios.title: The Shiny Tool
scenarios.situation: A study group adopts a new AI note-taking app that auto-summarizes lectures. It saves 20 minutes a week but its notifications and feed fragment every study session, and the summaries are shallow enough that members stop reading primary sources.
scenarios.prompt: Apply the craftsman approach to tool selection.
choices: Reject the tool: adopt a tool only if its positive impacts on the factors that matter to your deep work substantially outweigh its negative impacts. Twenty saved minutes do not buy back fragmented attention and abandoned primary sources.
Keep the tool — 20 minutes saved is 20 minutes saved.
Keep the tool but use it only on weekends.
Replace it with a different app that has nicer summaries.
scenarios.why: The craftsman approach to tool selection is the corrective to default adoption: a tool must earn its place by serving your deep work, and you must be willing to abandon tools that fail the test, however fashionable they are. Busyness is visible and deep work is not, so organizations — and study groups — drift toward tools that optimize the visible metric.
scenarios.hint: Add up the attention cost, not just the minutes saved.

scenarios.title: Blocking the Proof
scenarios.situation: Priya must master a difficult proof this week alongside classes, email, and a part-time job. She currently 'finds time when she can,' which means the proof gets the leftover scraps of her attention.
scenarios.prompt: How should she schedule it?
choices: Time-block: assign the proof fixed, defended blocks on her calendar — e.g. 90-minute morning blocks, phone in another room, one problem per block — and let shallow work fill the cracks. Deep work does not happen in found time; it happens in protected time.
Wait for a free weekend and binge the proof in one sitting.
Study the proof in 10-minute gaps between classes.
Read the proof's summary the night before she needs it.
scenarios.why: Time blocking converts intention into schedule: every deep task gets a defended block, and shallow obligations fit around the blocks rather than displacing them. The craftsman mindset runs through it — mastery comes from sustained, deliberate depth, not from finding the perfect technique or waiting for motivation.
scenarios.hint: If the proof only gets leftover attention, what quality of understanding will it get?

scenarios.title: The Capstone System
scenarios.situation: After months of reading about attention, Sam still runs on willpower: no shutdown time, phone on the desk, sessions that start 'whenever.' He asks you to help him build his own deep-work operating system.
scenarios.prompt: What does a complete personal system include?
choices: All of the load-bearing parts, assembled: the thesis accepted (why depth wins economically), deep/shallow sorting of his actual task list, the four rules operationalized, fixed shutdown time, time-blocked calendar, a digital-minimalism tool audit, an email/batch protocol, slow-productivity pacing across the semester, and a weekly review that measures deep hours and produced artifacts.
A stricter phone lock app and more willpower.
Copying someone else's exact schedule hour for hour.
Reading one more productivity book before starting.
scenarios.why: A deep-work operating system is not one technique — it is the thesis plus rules plus schedule plus tool audit plus communication protocol plus pacing, reviewed weekly against honest metrics (deep hours, artifacts produced). Slow productivity is the pacing layer: fewer obligations, done at a natural pace, with obsessive focus on quality — sustainable depth beats sprint-and-burn across a semester.
scenarios.hint: Which part of Sam's current setup would survive contact with the four rules?

lessons.title: Deep Work: Attention as a Technical Skill — Core concepts
concepts: The deep work hypothesis: as automation commoditizes routine work, cognitively demanding work grows more valuable — while the capacity for distraction-free concentration grows rarer. Value rises precisely because rarity rises.

Deep work pushes your cognitive limits and creates hard-to-replicate value; shallow work is logistical, interruptible, and easy to replicate — and knowledge work drifts shallow by default because busyness is visible and depth is not.
Attention residue: every task switch leaves part of your attention on the previous task. Interrupted sessions are not stitched-together fragments — each fragment runs on a fraction of your mind.
The craftsman mindset (from So Good They Can't Ignore You, 2012): stop asking what work can offer you; become so skilled you are valuable, and trust that control and meaning follow mastery.
Fixed-schedule productivity: fix the end of the workday and work backward. The constraint forces prioritization, saying no, and protecting deep blocks.

The four rules: work deeply, embrace boredom, quit the attention-fragmenting tools, drain the shallows. Time blocking, digital minimalism, batched communication, and slow productivity are the operating system built on top.

example.code:
# The seven-day attention audit (run this honestly)
mkdir -p ~/deepwork && cat > ~/deepwork/audit-week1.md <<'EOF'
# Attention audit — week of 2026-10-06
# Log each 30-min block: DEEP / SHALLOW / LOST
# Mon: ...
# Totals: deep=__ shallow=__ lost=__
EOF
cat ~/deepwork/audit-week1.md
example.walkthrough: Create the audit file and log every 30-minute block for seven days as deep (distraction-free, cognitively demanding), shallow (logistical, interruptible), or lost (fragmented beyond use). Most first-timers find fewer than five genuine deep hours in a week — that number, not your intentions, is your starting point.

pitfalls: Common trap: counting desk time as deep time. If the phone was on the desk, the session was shallow or lost — attention residue doesn't care about your intentions.
Common trap: adopting tools by default. The craftsman test is net impact on your deep work; fashionable tools that fragment attention fail it.
Common trap: the passion mindset — hunting for the perfect study technique instead of building rare skill through sustained depth.
Common trap: sprint-and-burn pacing. Slow productivity (fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality) sustains depth across a semester; all-nighters don't.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab: run the seven-day attention audit, then time-block next week around the deep hours you actually have.

Teach-back method: after each capstone milestone, explain what you built to someone (or a rubber duck) — gaps in your explanation are gaps in understanding.

lessons.title: Capstone: 90-Day Deep Work System — Build Guide
concepts: Milestone 1 — Foundation: scaffold the project, verify the toolchain works end-to-end before adding complexity.
Milestone 2 — Core: implement the central functionality. This is the demoable heart of the project.
Milestone 3 — Hardening: handle errors, add validation, make it robust enough to demo without fear.
Milestone 4 — Polish: README, diagrams, clean output. This is what separates 'homework' from 'portfolio'.
Testing each milestone: define 'done' as a verifiable behavior, not a feeling. Write the check before the code.
Narrative prep: for each milestone, prepare a 60-second explanation — what it does, why it matters, what was hard.

  ✓ Output verified against expected result
  ✓ Committed with a clear message
  ✓ README section updated

No milestone is done until all boxes check.

labs.title: The seven-day attention audit
labs.objective: Measure your real deep hours by logging every 30-minute block for a week — the baseline your whole system is built on.
steps: Create ~/deepwork/audit-week1.md with a header for the week and a line for each day.
For seven days, log every 30-minute block as DEEP (distraction-free, cognitively demanding), SHALLOW (logistical, interruptible), or LOST (fragmented beyond use).
Total your genuine deep hours. Write a one-paragraph response to the deep work hypothesis: do you accept it, and what changes if it's true?
Sort your recurring tasks into a deep list and a shallow list inside the same file.
Print the audit file to confirm totals and the response paragraph exist.

checks.hint: cat your audit file and confirm the deep/shallow/lost totals are filled in.
Verify the file exists and has content (wc -l or grep).

labs.title: Time-block your week: the personal operating system
labs.objective: Build a complete weekly system: fixed shutdown, defended deep blocks, batched shallow work, and a tool audit.
steps: Set a fixed shutdown time for every day and write it at the top of ~/deepwork/system.md.
Time-block next week: assign each cognitively demanding task a defended 60–90 minute block; batch shallow tasks into two windows per day.
Run the craftsman tool audit: list every app/tool you use, and mark keep/cut by net impact on your deep work.
Define your communication protocol: when you check messages, and what 'urgent' actually means.
Print system.md to confirm the shutdown time, blocks, audit, and protocol are all present.

checks.hint: cat system.md and confirm the fixed shutdown time is stated.
Confirm the time blocks and tool audit are present (grep for a block label).

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to master something genuinely difficult. How did you structure your effort?
behavioral.framework: STAR: the hard thing, the system (blocks, environment, metrics), the depth achieved, the outcome.
points: Describes a system, not just effort
pitfalls: 'I just worked harder'
No structure described

behavioral.prompt: How do you protect focus time in an environment full of interruptions?
behavioral.framework: Concrete mechanisms: shutdown rituals, batched communication, environment design, saying no.
pitfalls: 'I just ignore everyone'
No real mechanism

behavioral.prompt: Describe a tool or habit you deliberately quit because it was hurting your work.
behavioral.framework: The craftsman test: measured impact on deep work, the decision, what replaced it, the result.
pitfalls: Never quit anything
Quit without a replacement plan

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you plan a typical week.
behavioral.framework: Time blocking: deep blocks first, shallow batched, fixed shutdown; what gets protected and what gets cut.
points: Deep work scheduled, not hoped for
pitfalls: No plan / pure reactivity
Every hour 'flexible'

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you chose depth over speed — doing less, better.
behavioral.framework: Slow-productivity framing: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality; the tradeoff and the payoff.
pitfalls: Confuses slowness with depth
No payoff evidence

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle email and messages without letting them run your day?
behavioral.framework: Batched communication protocol: defined check times, sender expectations, what counts as urgent.
pitfalls: 'I check constantly just in case'
No protocol at all

behavioral.prompt: Describe a distraction-heavy period in your life and what you changed.
behavioral.framework: Before/after: the audit (honest numbers), the interventions, the measured change in deep hours.
pitfalls: Vague 'I got better'
Blames environment only

behavioral.prompt: What does 'done' mean for your learning — how do you know you've actually mastered something?
behavioral.framework: Artifacts not hours: what you produced (proofs re-derived, bugs found, systems built) as the depth metric.
pitfalls: Hours logged as the metric
'I read the chapter'

cheatsheet: The hypothesis: focus is getting rarer and more valuable at the same time.
Deep = distraction-free, cognitively demanding, hard to replicate. Shallow = logistical, interruptible, automatable.
Attention residue: every switch taxes the next task. Protect session starts.
Craftsman mindset: build rare skill; control and meaning follow mastery.
Fixed-schedule productivity: fix the shutdown, work backward.
Four rules: work deeply, embrace boredom, quit fragmenting tools, drain the shallows.
Slow productivity: fewer obligations, natural pace, obsessive quality.

glossary.def: Professional activity in distraction-free concentration that pushes cognitive limits; creates new value, hard to replicate.
Non-cognitively-demanding, logistical work, often done distracted; creates little new value, easy to replicate.
The portion of attention left on a previous task after switching, degrading performance on the new task.
Focus on what you can offer the world through rare skill, rather than what work can offer you.
Fixing the end of the workday and fitting everything into the available hours, forcing prioritization.
Do fewer things, work at a natural pace, obsess over quality — sustainable depth over sprint-and-burn.

checklist: I can state the deep work hypothesis with both drivers of rarity and both drivers of value.
I sorted my real task list into deep and shallow this week.
I know my genuine deep hours from the seven-day audit.
I have a fixed shutdown time and defended deep blocks.
I audited my tools with the craftsman test and cut the failures.

simulations.brief: Maya logged three hours of study, but her quiz score didn't move. Diagnose what actually happened in that session.

steps.symptom: Maya studied distributed systems for three hours. Her practice-quiz score is identical to yesterday's.
evidence: 4 chat threads, average reply latency 3 minutes
"I was studying the whole time, I swear."
options: She didn't try hard enough — the fix is more willpower
Attention residue: every switch left part of her mind on the previous task, so each fragment ran on a fraction of her attention
Distributed systems is simply too hard to learn in an afternoon
steps.explain: Attention residue is the mechanism: the brain doesn't instantly reallocate. Eleven switches means eleven partial minds, none of them fully on Raft consensus.

steps.symptom: Maya says the afternoon 'felt busy and productive' despite zero measurable progress.
evidence: "I was juggling a lot — it felt like real work."
options: Busyness is a reliable proxy for depth — she probably did learn something
Shallow work feels productive because motion is visible; depth is invisible until tested
She should study longer hours to compensate
steps.explain: Shallow work is logistical, interruptible, and easy to replicate — and it mimics the feeling of work. The test score is the honest instrument, not the feeling.

steps.symptom: Maya wants tomorrow to be different. Which intervention actually changes the structure of the session?
evidence: She has the same phone, same roommates, same chatty team
One 90-minute block on consensus algorithms, quiz score +20%
options: Promise herself she'll 'really focus this time'
Time-block the 90 minutes, phone in another room, single target written down, shutdown ritual at the end
Study the same material but take more detailed notes
steps.explain: Structure beats intention. Fixed-schedule productivity plus environment design — phone physically elsewhere, one target, a defined stop — is the system that makes depth the default.

simulations.debrief: Honest measurement (quiz scores, not hours logged) plus structural fixes (phone away, single target, time block) turn study time into actual skill. Attention is the bottleneck — train it like one.

simulations.title: The Shutdown Ritual
simulations.brief: It's 5:40 PM. Your deep block ended at 5:00 but the inbox is still pinging. Run the end of the day like a professional.

steps.text: 5:40 PM. Your planned stop time was 5:00. Three unread messages glow in the corner of your screen, and part of your brain is still chewing on the consensus bug. What do you do?

choices.label: Answer 'just one more email' — it'll only take five minutes
choices.feedback: Forty minutes later you're still in the inbox. The shutdown never happened, and the bug follows you to dinner.

choices.label: Run the shutdown ritual: capture open loops, review tomorrow's block, say the day is done
choices.feedback: You write down the bug's current state, block 9:00–10:30 tomorrow for it, and close the laptop. The ritual tells your brain the workday is over.

choices.label: Close the laptop abruptly and doomscroll on the couch
choices.feedback: The laptop is closed but the loops are open — you'll ruminate all evening. Shutdown is a procedure, not a lid position.

steps.text: 8:15 PM. You're on the couch and the consensus bug pops into your head again, uninvited. Tomorrow's 9 AM block has no defined target. What's the repair?

choices.label: Do a 5-minute capture now: write the bug state and tomorrow's single target on paper
choices.feedback: A late, partial ritual still beats none — the loop closes enough for sleep, and tomorrow has a target.

choices.label: Open the laptop 'just to jot it down' — and check the inbox while you're there
choices.feedback: The inbox reopens the loops you were trying to close. Tomorrow starts already fragmented.

steps.text: Shutdown complete: open loops captured, tomorrow's 9:00–10:30 block has one target (fix the Raft election timeout). Your phone buzzes — a teammate asking for 'a quick review tonight'. What now?

choices.label: Reply: 'I'll review it in my 11:00 shallow block tomorrow — send the link'
choices.feedback: Fixed-schedule productivity in action: the constraint forces the work into its proper shallow slot instead of eating your evening.

choices.label: Do the review now to be a team player
choices.feedback: One exception becomes the precedent. Tomorrow's deep block starts with residue from tonight.

simulations.debrief: A shutdown ritual is how you make the workday actually end: capture every open loop, assign tomorrow's deep block a single target, and let the constraint protect your evening. Recovery is part of depth.

simulations.title: Build the Deep Block
simulations.brief: Put the five moves of a proper 90-minute deep-work block in the order a professional runs them.

steps.context: You have 90 unscheduled minutes and one hard problem. Order the moves that turn those minutes into a real deep block.
items: Write down the single target for the block — one sentence
Clear the environment: phone in another room, tabs closed, notifications off
Set a visible timer for 90 minutes and start it
Work the single target with no switching until the timer ends
Log what you produced and where you stopped, then shut down

simulations.debrief: Target first, environment second, timer third — the block is a container you prepare before you enter. Logging at the end makes tomorrow's start instant instead of a 20-minute warm-up.

simulations.title: Attention Environment Audit
simulations.brief: A junior engineer shows you their 'focus setup'. Find the 3 attention leaks hiding in this configuration.

steps.config:
# focus.conf — 'my deep work setup'
phone_notifications = ON          # line 2
phone_location = desk, face-up   # line 3
chat_client = open, all channels unmuted  # line 4
timer = none                    # line 5
block_target = 'whatever feels important'  # line 6
door = closed                   # line 7
music = lo-fi playlist, lyrics-free       # line 8

issues.description: Phone notifications are ON — every buzz is a task-switch that leaves attention residue.
issues.fix: phone_notifications = OFF during deep blocks (or phone in another room).

issues.description: Phone on the desk face-up — mere presence of the phone degrades available cognitive capacity.
Chat client open with all channels unmuted — an always-on interruption firehose.
issues.fix: chat_client = closed during deep blocks; check in batched shallow slots.

simulations.debrief: Environment design beats willpower: notifications off, phone physically elsewhere, chat closed. Note lines 5–6 are also weak (no timer, vague target) but the three flagged lines are the active leaks.

simulations.title: The Interruption Storm
simulations.brief: You're 40 minutes into a deep block on a hard proof when your manager Slacks: 'quick call?'. Navigate the next ten minutes without losing the block.

steps.text: 40 minutes into the block. The proof is finally yielding. Slack: your manager — 'quick call?'. The message preview alone has already cost you some focus. What's the move?

choices.label: Reply instantly and jump on the call — managers outrank blocks
choices.feedback: The block is destroyed. Whatever the call was, it could have waited 50 minutes — and now the proof's state has to be rebuilt from scratch.

choices.label: Don't look. Finish the block, then reply in your next shallow slot
choices.feedback: You protect the remaining 50 minutes. If it were truly urgent, they'd call — Slack is by design non-urgent.

choices.label: Glance at the message to 'triage' whether it's urgent
choices.feedback: Triage IS the interruption — reading it loads their context into your working memory. Attention residue begins at the preview.

steps.text: The block is gone — you're context-switched and the proof's thread is lost. Damage control: what salvages the day?

choices.label: Log exactly where you stopped, then handle the interruption fully
choices.feedback: The log preserves the state; tomorrow's restart costs minutes instead of an hour. Partial credit for professional wreckage management.

choices.label: Try to 'quickly get back into it' between Slack replies
choices.feedback: Multitasking the recovery guarantees neither the proof nor the replies get a full mind. The residue compounds.

steps.text: Block complete — proof sketched, state logged. You open Slack: the manager's 'quick call' was a question your teammate already answered in-thread. Now you reply. What does the reply teach?

choices.label: 'Saw this after my focus block — glad it's resolved. For urgent things, call me; Slack waits until my shallow slots.'
choices.feedback: You train the organization: urgent = call, everything else = batched. Each defended block makes the next one easier to defend.

choices.label: Say nothing about the delay — just answer normally
choices.feedback: The block survived, but nobody learned the protocol. Next week the same ping arrives at minute 40 again.

simulations.debrief: Defending a block is a skill with two halves: the in-the-moment refusal to triage (triage is the interruption), and the after-action protocol you teach others. Urgent things arrive by phone; everything else waits for shallow time.

consoleSims.title: Lock Down the Focus Environment
consoleSims.brief: Your attention environment is a system you administer. Create the focus directory, add a blocklist file, and lock its permissions down.

tasks.instruction: Create the directory /home/user/focus — this is where deep-block artifacts live.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Create directory' form with PATH set to /home/user/focus.

tasks.instruction: Create the file /home/user/focus/blocklist.txt — your personal list of attention thieves to keep closed during blocks.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Create file' form with PATH set to /home/user/focus/blocklist.txt.

tasks.instruction: Set mode 600 on /home/user/focus/blocklist.txt — your blocklist is yours alone.
tasks.hint: Select the blocklist.txt row, then use the chmod form with mode 600.

consoleSims.debrief: Environment design is administration: dedicated directories for deep work, explicit blocklists, tight permissions. You don't negotiate with distractions mid-block — you configure them out beforehand.

consoleSims.title: Triage the Interruption Queue
consoleSims.brief: Every interruption is an incident. Run the queue like an on-call engineer: log it, assign it, move it — don't just absorb it.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'Phone buzzed 11 times during deep block' — interruptions get logged, not suffered silently.

params.title: Phone buzzed 11 times during deep block

tasks.hint: Use the 'New ticket' section: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P2.

tasks.instruction: Assign ticket INC-9001 to 'maya' — the pre-seeded VPN ticket is hers to drive.
tasks.hint: Use the Assign form with TICKET ID INC-9001 and ASSIGNEE maya.

tasks.instruction: Move INC-9001 to 'in-progress' — batched shallow work starts now, not during the next deep block.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Update status' form: INC-9001 → in-progress.

consoleSims.debrief: Logging interruptions as tickets does two things: it keeps them out of your working memory during deep blocks, and it gives you data — which interruptions recur, and which deserve a structural fix.

consoleSims.title: Ship the Daily Deep Block
consoleSims.brief: Treat your study system like a pipeline: trigger the day's build, fix the failing stage, approve the release of your notes.

tasks.instruction: Trigger a new build — this starts today's deep-work run with build and test green, deploy gated.
tasks.hint: Click the 'Trigger new build' button in the Pipeline section.

tasks.instruction: The 'test' stage is failing (your recall check flopped). Retry the test stage.
tasks.hint: Click Retry next to the test stage.

tasks.instruction: Set the pipeline variable FOCUS_HOURS to 4 — declare today's depth budget explicitly.
tasks.hint: Go to the Variables section and set KEY=FOCUS_HOURS, VALUE=4.

tasks.instruction: Approve the gated 'deploy' stage — ship today's notes and log the session.
tasks.hint: Click Approve next to the deploy stage.

consoleSims.debrief: A pipeline makes the abstract concrete: trigger (start the block), retry (re-drill what failed), variables (declare the budget), approve (publish the output). Systems beat intentions.

consoleSims.title: Configure the Focus Dashboard
consoleSims.brief: Set up the dashboard that tracks your deep-work practice: name it, set your timezone, and submit.

tasks.instruction: Set the site_name field to 'Deep Work HQ'.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Set site name' form with VALUE 'Deep Work HQ'.

tasks.instruction: Set the timezone field to 'America/New_York' so your block schedule renders correctly.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Set timezone' form with VALUE 'America/New_York'.

tasks.instruction: Submit the settings form to save your dashboard configuration.

consoleSims.debrief: What gets configured gets measured. A named dashboard in the right timezone is the home base your daily shutdown ritual reports to.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Workspace
terminalMissions.brief: Before a deep block, orient: list the workspace and read the study notes already waiting there.
objectives: List the files in the practice workspace
Read the study notes file to see what's already documented

checks.hint: Type: ls — the workspace listing includes notes.txt.
Type: cat notes.txt — the notes open with 'Linux essentials'.

terminalMissions.success_message: Workspace surveyed. Orientation is the cheapest part of a deep block — never skip it.

terminalMissions.title: Start the Attention Log
terminalMissions.brief: Honest measurement starts with a log. Create attention.txt and record today's deep-block entries.
objectives: Create attention.txt with your first deep-block entry
Append a second entry marking a completed block

checks.hint: Type: echo "block 1: 90 min consensus" > attention.txt (output is empty on success — that's normal).
Type: echo "block 2: 60 min raft log" >> attention.txt to append a second line.
Type: cat attention.txt to verify both entries are logged.

terminalMissions.success_message: Attention log started. What gets logged gets managed — this file is now your honest instrument.

terminalMissions.title: Count the Switches
terminalMissions.brief: Add three DISTRACTION lines to your attention log, then measure: how many lines, and how many were distractions?
objectives: Append three DISTRACTION entries to attention.txt
Count total lines in the log
Search the log for DISTRACTION entries

checks.hint: Append a distraction, e.g.: echo "DISTRACTION: checked phone" >> attention.txt — do it three times (once is enough to tick this check).
Type: wc -l attention.txt — the output ends with the filename.
Type: grep DISTRACTION attention.txt to list every distraction line.

terminalMissions.success_message: Measured. The ratio of deep lines to DISTRACTION lines is the score that matters — hours logged mean nothing next to it.

terminalMissions.title: Read the Edges
terminalMissions.brief: Review sessions start at the edges: the first lines set the intention, the last lines show where you stopped.
objectives: Read the first two lines of attention.txt
Read the last line of attention.txt

checks.hint: Type: head -n 2 attention.txt — the first entries appear.
Type: tail -n 3 attention.txt — your latest entries (including distractions) appear.

terminalMissions.success_message: Edges read. Every shutdown ritual ends by reading where you stopped — tomorrow's start is already written.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Daily Goal
terminalMissions.brief: Write tomorrow's single target as a hash commitment — a tamper-evident seal on your intention.
objectives: Hash your daily goal string with sha256sum
Verify the goal text appears in the hash output

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum finish chapter 4 — the output echoes your goal text after the real hash.

terminalMissions.success_message: Goal sealed. A commitment you can verify beats a resolution you can quietly rewrite.

terminalMissions.title: Check the Environment
terminalMissions.brief: A deep block needs a clean environment. Verify who you are, where you are, and what home is set to.
objectives: Confirm your shell identity and environment
Print your home directory from the environment

checks.hint: Type: ps — in this sandbox it prints your environment, including USER=candidate.
Type: echo $HOME — the shell expands it to /home/candidate.

terminalMissions.success_message: Environment verified. Professionals check the runway before takeoff — even a mental one.

terminalMissions.title: Verify Reachability
terminalMissions.brief: Before a block that needs the network (docs, repos), confirm DNS resolves and the path is clean.
objectives: Confirm zero packet loss with ping

checks.hint: Type: dig interstitiumlabs.dev — the ANSWER SECTION shows the resolved address.
Type: ping interstitium — the summary reports 0% packet loss.

terminalMissions.success_message: Network verified. Eliminate the environment as a variable before you blame your focus.
